newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bombing raises security concern after NATO raid.
newsitem.headline: Bombing raises security concern after NATO raid.

text.p: A bomb exploded outside offices of international monitors in Bosnia's Serb-controlled territory, but the blast was not seen as part of a revenge campaign against a NATO raid on suspected war criminals, an international envoy said.
The explosion on Sunday evening destroyed an OSCE pickup truck but caused no casualties in the eastern town of Zvornik, a United Nations spokesman said.
International envoys and the NATO-led peace force said there was no sign that the explosion in Zvornik was part of an organised campaign of retaliation for last Thursday's NATO raid.
"We do not see a widespread, orchestrated security problem. We see isolated incidents," said Duncan Bullivant, spokesman for the High Representative to Bosnia, Carlos Westendorp.
U.N. spokesman Liam McDowall said: "There was a sizeable explosion about 30 metres (yards) from the building which houses both the U.N. and the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe.
"The blast completely destroyed one OSCE vehicle and damaged a second civilian vehicle nearby," he told Reuters.

The bombing came after NATO's swoop on two Serbs indicted for war crimes in the northwest Prijedor region. One suspect was arrested and a second was shot dead after he opened fire on British soldiers trying to detain him.
The NATO operation last week broke new ground for the alliance which had previously ruled arresting suspects only if its troops happened to encounter them.
NATO had hesitated in the past to carry out arrests partly out of concern that its peacekeeping troops could be exposed to violent reprisals and relations with rival armies could be jeopardised.
Nationalist Serb leaders condemned the NATO operation but have refrained from inciting retaliatory attacks.
U.N. police monitors had suffered minor harassment in Zvornik over the weekend but there were no plans to evacuate international staff from Serb territory, officials said.
Serb leaders were also angered by the sentencing on Monday of Dusan Tadic, a Serb convicted of atrocities by the U.N. war crimes tribunal for former Yugoslavia. Tadic was sentenced to 20 years.

"This is a political sentence...We are very bitter that care was not taken to put this trial on a better political foundation," said Momcilo Krajisnik, the Serb member of Bosnia's multi-ethnic collective presidency.
Krajisnik is a close ally of former Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic, who is also wanted for war crimes.
Krajisnik and other hardline nationalists attended a funeral on Sunday for Simo Drljaca, the former police chief in Prijedor who shot a British soldier in the leg while resisting arrest.
Drljaca, a loyal servant of Karadzic, was accused of helping orchestrate expulsions of Moslems and Croats from the Prijedor region early in the Bosnian war in 1992.

The hardliners loyal to Karadzic have been waging a battle for power with Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic, who has accused them of profiting from smuggling rackets at the expense of ordinary people.
Plavsic and her rival, Krajisnik, met on Monday in Banja Luka in an attempt to resolve their conflict.
The High Representative's office said Serb television coverage of the power struggle and the NATO operation was full of "disinformation and outrageous comments".

Diplomats said major powers were considering jamming the Serb television signal if necessary and broadcasting Radio Free Europe or the Voice of America to Bosnia in a bid to counter reports coming out of Karadzic's media.

NATO spokesman Major Chris Riley denied allegations in Serb media that Drljaca was "murdered". He said an autopsy showed that Drljaca was hit by four bullets and was not shot in the back or in the head.
